sports.title: Depth Delivers: UTEP men win in Cancun without top scorers
sports.description: The UTEP men's basketball team has raved about its depth early in the 2026-27 season. On their first long road trip of the year at the Cancun Challenge against the College of Charleston, they got to live it. Playing in Mexico without their two leading scorers, Cam McDaniels and Youssouf Traore, who did not make the trip because of injuries, UTEP overcame the challenge and the now-4-2 Cougars, 80-69. The 5-1 Miners did it with a revamped lineup and depth, led by the most likely player, point guard Leif Moeller, and normal reserve Reid Cason. With the win, UTEP will play Eastern Michigan on Wednesday, Nov. 25 at 6:30 p.m. MT. UTEP made this look fairly routine, taking control with a 12-2 run that helped stake the Miners to a 42-26 lead they saw home. In building the first-half lead that proved decisive, the Miners held Charleston to 19% shooting (1-of-14 from 3-point range) and held the Cougars without a field goal for the final 7:42 of the half. Charleston got going a bit in the second half, but UTEP had the margin it needed. UTEP was consistent offensively all game, finishing at 54% to Charleston’s 34%. The Miners didn’t blink down the stretch against the Cougars’ press to win their fifth consecutive game. As he was brought in to do, the sophomore Moeller was the glue with 14 points and 10 rebounds. Cason, getting his first start as a Miner, scored 12 points on 6-of-8 shooting and had six rebounds. Freshman Donovan Criss continued the impressive start to his UTEP career, scoring 13 points to go with three assists. UTEP won bench points 31-16 despite having two normal reserves, Cason and Jace Whiting, in the starting lineup. Where the Miners struggled was getting outscored at the free-throw line, as the Cougars were 29-of-37 to UTEP’s 15-of-20, as both Augusto Cassia and Cason fouled out as part of the Miners’ 27 fouls. The Miners won points off turnovers 18-11 despite giving the ball away 16 times to Charleston’s 14. sports.title: Pistons down Magic, Celtics hold off Wizards
sports.description: Detroit's Daniss Jenkins and Ausar Thompson combine to block Orlando's Anthony Black (Rich Storry) The Detroit Pistons shrugged off the injury absence of Cade Cunningham to keep their NBA Cup hopes alive on Tuesday with a gritty 104-86 road victory over the Orlando Magic. Isaiah Joe led Detroit's scoring with 21 points after nailing five three-pointers as five Pistons players finished in double figures. Orlando, who could have booked their place in the knockout rounds with a victory, started brightly to take a 22-16 lead after the first quarter. But a devastating scoring burst from Detroit in the second quarter, outscoring Orlando 32-14, changed the contest. Detroit took a 48-36 lead into half-time and maintained a double-digit cushion for most of the remainder of the game. "I thought our defense was elite tonight," Pistons coach J.B. Bickerstaff said. "On a night where we were down some offense, we knew we were going to have to hang our hat on the defensive end of the floor and I love the way that everybody contributed. "Everbody bought into it and that was the best part. We knew it was going to be a gritty, physical game, but our guys did a great job." Orlando lead the Eastern Conference Group A with a 3-1 record while the Pistons are in third place on 2-1 behind the Toronto Raptors. The Boston Celtics all but locked up their place in the quarter-finals after holding off a furious rally from the Washington Wizards to score a 131-116 win on the road in the East's Group C. Jayson Tatum scored 41 points for the Celtics while Paul George added 28 and Neemias Queta 21 to halt Boston's four-game losing streak. The Celtics looked to be cruising towards a crushing win after racing into a 34-point lead just before half-time. But the Wizards hit back to outscore Boston 40-24 in the third quarter and got to within seven points of the lead late in the fourth at 119-112. Boston regrouped down the stretch and a pair of three-pointers from Baylor Scheierman saw the Celtics pull clear. "We had a tough week last week for various different reasons," Tatum said of Boston's run of four straight losses before Tuesday. "But you can't change what happens. We always try to focus on today," he told NBC. Tatum added he was not surprised by the Wizards' rally. "No lead is safe and they get paid to play basketball too, right?" he said. "They’ve got a lot of talent over there so it was just a case of trying to weather the storm." rcw/pst

sports.description: The USGA and R&A provided a considerable update to the golf ball rollback decision. Getty Images The latest twist in the golf ball rollback saga has arrived. Late last week, the USGA and R&A quietly released a “ notice to manufacturers ” indicating they have identified two paths to limit distance gains in professional golf and are targeting approval of those changes in time for the start of the new PGA Tour schedule in 2028. At first glance, the changes outlined by the governing bodies aim to limit distance gains for pro players with the driver and golf ball, but appear to fall short of the distance drops targeted by the golf ball rollback standard initially pursued back in 2023. But let’s hold on for a second. If you’re a golfer with a normal degree of exposure to governing body minutiae, you’ve probably got no idea what I just said. So let’s get you the goods without the headache in Q&A form. 1. What’s the backstory? The USGA and R&A have been looking to curb distance in pro golf for years … but as it turns out, it’s pretty hard to curb distance! Players hate it. Club companies hate it. Regular golfers hate it. The governing bodies don’t even seem to like it. In fact, it might be said that curbing distance in golf is a lot like eating chard — if it’s so good for you, why does it taste like that?! The USGA and R&A are unusual in that they are self-aware enough to recognize their chard-iness. They have tried very hard to find a solution to the distance problem that will satisfy everyone or, at least, annoy everyone the least. First the USGA and R&A pitched a golf ball rollback that would only affect Tour pros. That led to a mutiny. Then, in late 2023, they pitched a rollback for all golfers , pro and recreational. Another mutiny. THEN , in early 2026, they announced a sudden agreement with the PGA Tour to work toward new solutions to curb distance while pushing back the deadline for the rollback-for-all to 2030. No mutiny this time … well, except for all the regular golfers who understood a rollback was necessary to preserve the sport in its purest form. Among that crew? Yep, you guessed it: Mutiny. Now we have last week’s announcement, which appears to show plans to cut back driver AND golf ball distance … but by what sounds like a smaller margin than the original all-golfer rollback. That’s good news if you didn’t want to lose 15 yards every time you teed off at Bethpage with your buddies. It’s good news if you’re a pro golfer who didn’t want to lose 15 yards at the Masters. And it’s good news if you’re the USGA and R&A and you know you’ve gotta do something to stop the steady creep of distance increases. 2. What is the change the USGA and R&A are promoting? Basically, they want to make their equipment tests harder to pass. Right now, the equipment companies have wiggle room in how their golf balls and drivers get tested. technology.title: Dell and HPE both say they’ve become ‘different companies’
technology.description: Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.” The two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different company” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.” On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.” HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player. Dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a big difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure company. Clarke said he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead. Dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with” “Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.” HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the company’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent. The CEO said HPE expects better growth ahead, because new server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year. Dell is also optimistic that AI buyers will spend on kit beyond servers and GPUs and updated its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion, $10 billion above its previous forecasts and up 78 percent year over year. ®

technology.title: AI godfather Yann LeCun torches Anthropic CEO over AI gatekeeping
technology.description: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is taking heat from AI luminary Yann LeCun, one of the founding fathers of modern machine learning, because of the Claudefather's fear-mongering around open-weights models, which also happen to compete with his products. In an X post this week, LeCun likened the Amodei's advocacy to a “new form of medieval obscurantism.” “Dario’s spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal, and he would stay in control,” LeCun wrote in response to a now three-year-old video posted to the platform in which Amodei warned US Congress members about the dangers of open-weights models, the use of which could not be monitored or policed. “He left OpenAI because he wasn’t going to have control. It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma.” LeCun is one of the most influential names in AI and ML. His team is credited with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the late ’80s during his time at Bell Labs. He later oversaw the development of Meta’s Llama herd of models as chief AI scientist before shifting gears away from LLMs to world model architectures like JEPA. He has also been a strong proponent of open source AI development and open models. Of the major model houses, Anthropic has taken the most hostile position against the adoption of open-weights models. Despite advocating against the unregulated diffusion of open models for years, Anthropic’s fearmonger-in-chief has maintained that the company isn’t opposed to them. “Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post earlier this year. The executive has instead fomented fears over their potential misuse. “Open-weights models — it does not matter whether they come from China or anywhere else — do potentially present a higher risk than closed models, because it is very difficult to apply guardrails to them or monitor their usage, and, once weights are released, they cannot be withdrawn,” the blog post read. Amodei has repeatedly hammered these talking points over the past several years, including in the Senate hearing that solicited LeCun’s post. technology.title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?

Tackling Riemann The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. technology.description: Inception, a new data theft and extortion gang that security researchers have theorized is a rebrand of the ShinyHunters group, “reject[s] this attribution” and claims it has no affiliation with any prior cybercrime enterprise. In a lengthy statement posted Tuesday and shared on X, the extortionists insist that they are a new group, with new operators, and that their alleged social engineering attacks aren’t copying anyone - but rather just abusing the weakest link in an organization’s security: “a human being holding a phone.” The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very likely ShinyHunters with a different name . Okta’s researchers based their analysis on the two groups’ shared infrastructure, plus Inception’s nearly identical tactics: voice phishing , during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests. Inception apparently took offense to this. “We would like to address this once, clearly, and only once,” the crims' statement says. “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.” The gang argues that its overlapping domain registrars, hosting providers, and DNS services don’t prove anything. These are commodity services, “available to anyone who can pay for them,” Inception wrote. Plus, their similar methodologies don't necessarily make Inception a reboot. “That is not theft of tradecraft,” they wrote. “It is acknowledgment of a good idea – the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit.” “Inception is a new group, with new operators, our own objectives, and our own name,” the statement continues. “What we share with the past is plumbing.” To be fair, the new crime crew has every reason to distance itself from ShinyHunters. That gang’s September FBI hack - plus several earlier digital heists during which the criminals stole information belonging to millions of people, including cancer patients , university and K-12 students - put a massive target on its collective backs. And while at least three ShinyHunters suspects were arrested in September and October, there's no confirmation that authorities have dismantled the entire operation. Plus, as a ShinyHunters spokesperson told The Register in an earlier interview, they and others in the crew started off as GnosticPlayers before rebranding as ShinyHunters in 2020 - so a reboot isn’t beyond the realm of possibility. Inception, for its part, says it “will not comment further on the ghost of ShinyHunters,” and it has its own work to do. And by work, it means copying ShinyHunters' playbook, stealing corporate data, and extorting victim companies for massive sums of money.®

science.title: SpaceX launches secretive spy satellites from California for US Space Force (video)
science.description: null SpaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT) , carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month. While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities. (Image credit: SpaceX) About two and a half minutes after liftoff, Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued toward low Earth orbit with the classified payload. The booster, meanwhile, began a descent toward SpaceX's Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean, where it touched down approximately eight and a half minutes after launch. Tuesday's launch marked the 29th flight for this Falcon 9 booster, B1081, which previously launched NASA 's Crew-7 astronaut mission to the International Space Station , the PACE and EarthCARE science satellites , two other classified Space Force launches (USSF-153 and USSF-481), and 16 Starlink missions. Previous classified Space Force launches have fueled speculation about the possible deployment of SpaceX's Starshield satellites, which are designed for national security applications. Starshield is an adapted spacecraft design developed from SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation that supports military operations with capabilities like Earth observation and secure communications. SpaceX has not confirmed whether USSF-266 is carrying Starshield spacecraft. USSF-266 follows three other classified Space Force missions launched by SpaceX from Vandenberg earlier this month: USSF-432 on Nov. 6, USSF-627 on Nov. 11 and USSF-317 on Nov. 20, as well as a National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) launch, NROL-136, on Nov. 22. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
science.description: null On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space . (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control. The first Aerobee sounding rocket launched on Nov. 24, 1947 under a project led by the U.S. Navy. (Image credit: U.S. Navy) Why it mattered Billed as the " most successful sounding rocket of the space age ," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so. "The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview . "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds." An Aerobee suborbital sounding rocket of the type designed to study Earth's atmosphere. (Image credit: NMMSH) While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space , many more made successful launches in the decades that followed. Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight . More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985. Want more space history? science.title: Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom
science.description: 5 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit, cruises past Mars in this artist’s concept, demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space. Credit: NASA/Jonathan North NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time. Experts from across the agency, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland for a major SR-1 mission design review in October. Several key decisions were made, propelling the mission from an early concept toward a defined spacecraft design. “SR-1 marks a pivotal step in how we travel through the solar system,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “This mission will be the first freight run on the railroad of the solar system, and the decisions we’re making now are laying the tracks for every nuclear-powered spacecraft that follows.” Planned for launch in late 2028, SR-1 will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall , a capsule carrying three next-generation helicopters, to Mars. Once deployed, the helicopters will study Martian geology and climate history, explore new terrain, and search for signs of subsurface ice. As NASA prepares for more ambitious exploration missions, future spacecraft and surface operations will require significantly more power than current systems can provide, particularly in environments where sunlight is limited or unavailable. SR-1 will demonstrate how fission power can enable long-duration missions, pave the way for reliable surface power systems to support NASA’s future Moon Base , and enable exploration deeper into the solar system. Key design decisions The SR-1 Freedom spacecraft design has evolved since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman first introduced the concept in March at the agency’s Ignition event, where leadership shared plans to develop a fission-powered spacecraft in time for the next Mars launch window. One significant change is to use a shorter boom than the one shown in early illustrations. The boom separates the reactor from the spacecraft’s main body, known as the Power and Propulsion Element. The shorter boom will reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design. Planned for launch in late 2028, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall to Mars. This infographic explains the components of the spacecraft. Credit: NASA/David Lam NASA and DOE experts also determined that improvements in shielding and spacecraft design will allow the reactor to operate closer to the rest of the spacecraft. science.title: 1st-ever detection of a dying star's 'final nuclear heartbeat' challenges what we know about our sun's eventual death
science.description: null As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper. New observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed. NASA Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) researcher Raghvendra Sahai, who led the investigation, explained the shape the ALMA observations took: "It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models. We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas." Sun-like stars "die" when they run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means that the fusion of hydrogen to helium ceases in the stellar core, and because this nuclear process is a star's main energy source, the star no longer has the outward push to support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the star's core collapses to create a stellar remnant called a white dwarf , the outer layers where hydrogen is still fusing to form helium swell out. This expansion leads to a relatively short-lived " red giant " phase. Eventually, these outer layers will cool and disperse, leaving the central white dwarf surrounded by a so-called "planetary nebula" shell of debris. During the red giant phase, as the stellar core is surrounded by shells of hydrogen and helium, these layers are occasionally rocked by flares in nuclear activity called thermal pulses. During these episodes, stellar material is flung into space. To better understand this phase in stellar evolution, the team focused ALMA on a star called IRAS 06530-0213, located around 12,000 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros. This revealed a giant ring of gas that appears to be a frozen fossil of the star's last thermonuclear flare-up. This thermonuclear fossil rings an hourglass-shaped planetary nebula in the act of forming. "Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star's death throes," Sahai said. "It's the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action." science.title: Double asteroid solar eclipse caught on camera | Space photo of the day for Nov. 24, 2026
science.description: null (Image credit: ESA) A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another. What is it? The image shows the Didymos double asteroid system , which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos. The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its orbit and thus the trajectory of the entire two-asteroid system. Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Why is it incredible? For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth. But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid , meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet. Hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

science.title: China's Shenzhou-24 mission launches 1st international astronaut to Tiangong space station
science.description: null China has launed an international astronaut to its Tiangong space station today (Nov. 24) for the first time ever, marking a significant milestone for international participation in the Chinese space program. A Long March 2F rocket lifted off with the Shenzhou-24 crew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT and 8:18 a.m. Beijing time on Nov. 25). You can watch the liftoff live here at Space.com, courtesy of China Central Television (CCTV). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026. (Image credit: CCTV) Shenzhou-24 is China's 18th crewed spaceflight to date and its 12th astronaut mission to Tiangong , a three-module station that the nation finished assembling in low Earth orbit in late 2022. Those numbers may sound rather prosaic. But today's flight makes history, marking the first time that China has ever launched a foreign national to space. That trailblazer is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces who is the first person from his country ever to reach orbit. (Adventurer Namira Salim is the first Pakistani ever to fly to the final frontier, doing so on a Virgin Galactic suborbital mission in October 2023 .) China and Pakistan began paving Ali's path to Tiangong in February 2025 , with the signing of a spaceflight cooperation agreement in Islamabad. Pakistan then selected two astronaut candidates, who traveled to China for training. We didn't learn which Pakistani astronaut was picked for Shenzhou-24 until Monday night (Nov. 23), when China announced the mission's crew. This is not out of the ordinary, by the way; China generally doesn't reveal the identity of Shenzhou astronauts until the day before launch. This is in keeping with the nation's broader spaceflight ethos, which prizes keeping things close to the vest. Ali is flying as a payload specialist. The other Shenzhou-24 astronauts are commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi. Tang also flew on the Shenzhou-12 and Shenzhou-17 missions, which launched in June 2021 and October 2023, respectively. He will be the first person to visit Tiangong three times, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. Shenzhou-24 will be the first spaceflight for Wu. Tang and Wu are expected to live aboard Tiangong for six months, the usual Shenzhou rotation. But Ali will stay in orbit for just a week or so, coming back down to Earth with Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying of the Shenzhou-23 mission, which launched on May 24 . According to the South China Morning Post, the third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will stay behind when Ali leaves, living aboard Tiangong until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore become the first Chinese astronaut ever to spend a year in orbit, a milestone that will allow China to prep for long-duration missions to the moon and other deep-space locales.

science.title: Russia launches Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station (video)
science.description: null Russia's latest freighter is on its way to the International Space Station. The robotic Progress 97 cargo craft launched atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov. 24) at 5:17 a.m. EST (1013 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Baikonur time), carrying several tons of supplies for the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. If all goes to plan, Progress 97 will arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Nov. 26), docking with its Poisk module. But the freighter won't stay at that particular locale for long. A Russian Soyuz rocket launches the uncrewed Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station from Baikonur Cosmodrome, Kazakhstan on Nov. 24, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The cosmonauts currently living on the ISS — Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov — will unload Progress 97 through Poisk. But the freighter will then hop over to a different port, according to journalist and space historian Anatoly Zak: the aft one of the PrK transfer tunnel, which leads to Russia's Zvezda service module. The PrK port is the best site for engine burns that boost the orbit of the ISS, a service that Progress freighters regularly provide. But Progress 97 cannot unload its cargo through that port because the PrK transfer tunnel has been sealed off, due to an ongoing air leak that was first documented in 2019. Progress-97 is therefore "the first cargo mission scheduled to unload its cargo and perform orbit corrections of the ISS at different docking ports," Zak wrote on the site he runs, RussianSpaceWeb.com. Progress 96 cargo spacecraft packed with science and supplies approaches the International Space Station for a docking on Sept. 19, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The Progress 97 mission, which Russia calls Progress MS-36, was originally expected to launch this past August, according to Zak. But the liftoff was pushed back several times, most significantly by the collapse of the service platform at Baikonur's Site 31 in November 2025. It took Russia about three months to repair the platform, leading to a series of delays. Progress 97 will likely stay docked to the ISS for about six months, after which it will be loaded up with trash and sent home to burn up in Earth's atmosphere . Japan's HTV-X vehicle and Northrop Grumman's Cygnus spacecraft are similarly expendable. The only currently operational ISS cargo craft that's reusable is SpaceX's Dragon capsule, which makes parachute-aided ocean splashdowns at the end of its missions.

science.title: Severe eczema healed by novel immune-calming pill in clinical trial
science.description: Eczema causes itchy, inflamed rashes on the skin Evgeniia Gordeeva/Getty Images Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected. “It definitely looks promising,” says Gayle Ross at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Read more Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13. Advertisement In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is effective , it has had limited uptake in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage. Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter In the clinical trial , 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks. Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average 72 per cent reduction in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial. “These results exceeded our expectations,” said Terence Rooney , the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a webcast on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end. “It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross. science.title: November's full moon rises tonight! Here's how to see the Beaver Moon supermoon
science.description: null Get ready stargazers! The full "Beaver supermoon" rises in the eastern sky, offering up a spectacular display shortly after sunset tonight (Nov. 24). Here's what you need to know. November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk passes opposite the sun in our sky, making it appear fully lit from our perspective. The November full moon is often referred to as the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the small mammals are hard at work building their lodges in preparation for the winter. Viewers in the U.S. can even get a detailed look at the full moon ahead of local moonrise thanks to a free supermoon livestream from the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP), starting at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) today. The stream will feature live views of the lunar disk captured from the VTP's robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, weather permitting. The Beaver Moon is also set to be a dazzling supermoon , because it turns full as the natural satellite passes within 90% of perigee , when it is at its closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit. A supermoon's proximity can make it appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than the most distant full moon of the year, which is colloquially known as a "micro-moon". When to see the Beaver Moon November's full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. at the moment it turns full. Instead, viewers in America should look out for the moon shortly after sunset on Nov. 24, as it looms low over the eastern horizon. A supermoon can make for a spectacular sight when caught close to the horizon. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Try covering the lunar disk with your thumb to block out the worst of its glare, and you may just be able to spot to blue-white lights of the Pleiades open star cluster glimmering less than 10 degrees away — roughly the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length. If you miss the full moon on Nov. 24, don't worry as the moon will appear full to the casual observer for a couple more nights, so there's no excuse to miss it! Remember to check out Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location. What should I expect from the November supermoon? You may see the moon turn a striking orange-yellow hue as it rises because sunlight reflected from its disk passes through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters shorter bluer wavelengths of light and allows more red and orange light to reach our eyes in a process called Rayleigh scattering. Check out our full Celestron Nexstar 4SE review for more. science.title: Eruption Extends Iwo Jima’s Beach
science.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Eruption Extends Iwo Jima’s… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search October 26 November 11 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison October 26 November 11 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison October 26 November 11 Curtain Toggle 2-Up A volcanic eruption in the shallows near Iwo Jima has extended the Japanese island’s famed black sand beaches, at least temporarily. Signs of unrest began in late October 2026. On October 27, seismic sensors recorded a sharp uptick in activity, and Japan’s Meteorological Agency reported that the first photographs of the eruption were captured. Soon after, sensors on several satellites began to capture an array of observations. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured the left image on October 26, when the coast was still quiet. On November 11, Landsat 9 got its first clear view of the land the submarine volcano has built (right). A shortwave-infrared signature, a sign of the eruption’s heat, is shown in orange. A faint gray volcanic plume drifts southeast of the vent, and a streak of floating pumice stretches across the water in the same direction. A false-color backscatter radar image from the NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite offered an even earlier look at the eruption. On October 28, despite heavy cloud cover, the radar detected a large disturbance in the water in the same area that erupted in December 2023. When the clouds cleared in early November, the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors on NASA and NOAA satellites also captured signs of the ongoing eruption’s volcanic plumes and infrared signature . Japan’s Coast Guard released a report on November 16 confirming the formation of new land connected to the pre-existing beach. The eruption appears to have added roughly 50 hectares (125 acres) of new beach, about the area of 90 American football fields. That would enlarge the island by about 1.7 percent. The new land adjoins the southeast beach where American troops landed on February 19, 1945, beginning one of the bloodiest battles in the history of the U.S. Marines. The location of the eruption is no surprise to scientists. In addition to the 2023 eruption off the southeast coast, Iwo Jima had an eruption off its west coast in August 2025, said Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. science.title: Will astronauts farm on the moon? Scientists successfully grow potatoes in simulated lunar dust
science.description:
Julian Dossett is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He primarily covers the rocket industry and space exploration and, in addition to science writing, contributes travel stories to New Mexico Magazine. In 2022 and 2024, his travel writing earned IRMA Awards. Previously, he worked as a staff writer at CNET. He graduated from Texas State University in San Marcos in 2011 with a B.A. in philosophy. He owns a large collection of sci-fi pulp magazines from the 1960s.

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon. To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement . "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon." To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith , the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions. The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil. Oregon State University researchers David Handy and Aymeric Goyer studying potatoes grown in lunar regolith. (Image credit: Aymeric Goyer/David Handy/OSU) "We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement. The idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth. NASA funding supported this research.
